description: We're passionate about tech applied to real-world problems, especially agriculture and satellite data. Looking to add people with experience in data science/geospatial analysis, backend (APIs), UX design, and, if possible, agronomy knowledge. If you're excited about using NASA open data to solve a real challenge in the field, join our team.
summary:
Qullqa is a community digital twin that helps Andean farming families decide together what to plant. We built an installable web app, piloted in the Colca Valley, Peru. Families mark their plots with GPS and tap cards for what matters: income, risk, soil, or feed. Qullqa simulates every three-season rotation against 44 years of weather, using NASA POWER, GPM IMERG, MODIS and SRTM, plus farmers’ own field observations. It then finds the community plan that benefits everyone, penalizing neighbors repeating the same crop, under one rule: no family ends up worse than its best solo plan. Gains are shared with the Shapley value, expressed as ayni, Andean reciprocal work.

This turns NASA data into plot-level rotation plans coordinated across neighbors. Smallholders often rotate alone, or not at all: pests build up, soil depletes, prices crash. In simulation (120 synthetic families on 20 real plots), family income more than doubled and seasons with heavy losses fell from 3 in 10 to under 1 in 20.

As families join, Qullqa becomes a living map of Andean farming. With their consent, our admin panel already turns anonymized data into risk maps showing where frost and pests hit hardest, so authorities can direct canals, soil support and technical help. Data is never sold.
details:
What it does

Qullqa is a community digital twin. Think of it as a working copy of a community’s plots, climate and soil, where families can try out planting plans before anyone plants anything. Most farming tools advise one farm at a time. We plan for a whole neighbourhood of plots at once, because the things that ruin a harvest do not stop at a property line. Disease moves from plot to plot. The irrigation water comes from one canal. The price depends on what the whole valley takes to market. Our pilot is the Chivay, Yanque and Coporaque corridor in the Colca Valley, Peru, at 3,400 to 3,900 metres.

How it works

First, the data. NASA POWER gives us daily weather going back to 1981, corrected for the elevation of each plot. GPM IMERG fixes POWER’s rainfall, which was underestimating the Colca. It went from about 220 to about 380 mm a year, which matches what the valley actually receives. MODIS gives vegetation vigour (NDVI) and night temperatures on the terraces, so we know where frost bites hardest. SRTM gives relief and slope. We also use sources that are not NASA, and we always say so: SoilGrids for soils, ESA WorldCover for where cropland is, and NOAA for El Niño years.

Second, the farmer fills in what satellites cannot see at the scale of one plot. A family marks its plot by standing at each corner with GPS. The app averages the readings, draws the boundary, calculates the area, and closes the shape when they come back to the first corner. They also report frosts, harvests, soil moisture using the fist test, slope with the phone’s inclinometer, and a photo of crop cover. The harvests they record feed back and correct the model.

Third, the engine simulates every rotation possible across three seasons, running each one against 44 years of real weather. It calculates soil water day by day with the FAO 56 method, plus frost, erosion and expected yield, and scores each rotation on eight things: water, risk of losing the harvest, organic matter, nitrogen, erosion, pests, income and forage.

Fourth, each family says what matters to them by tapping one or two cards: earn more, do not lose the harvest, care for the land, or feed for the animals.

Fifth, and this is the part that makes Qullqa different, the system looks for the plan that works best for everyone together. It penalises neighbours all planting the same crop, which is what causes prices to collapse, pests to spread, irrigation to peak and soil to wash downstream. One rule governs the whole search: no family can end up worse off than with its own best plan alone.

Finally, if coordinating creates a surplus, it gets shared using the Shapley value from game theory, and we express it as ayni, the Andean practice of reciprocal work. That means work days, water turns or seed, not cash. Every family receives three options, which are what they plant today, their best plan on their own, and the plan with their neighbours. Each one explains why, which data it rests on, what risks to watch, and how confident the recommendation is.

What families get out of it

A rotation plan built on four decades of climate for their own plot, which no smallholder has access to today. And protection that only works collectively: fewer shared pests, a steadier price, lower irrigation peaks, less erosion downstream. Because nobody can end up worse off, joining is a reasonable decision, not an act of faith.

What we found in simulation

These are simulations, not field results. We built 12 synthetic communities on top of 20 real plot boundaries that we traced on satellite imagery of the lower terraces of Yanque. The plots run from 0.19 to 1.56 hectares, 12 hectares in total, between 3,431 and 3,441 metres, with about five neighbours each. That gave us 120 families of roughly 1.2 hectares, and we simulated every plan against real weather from 1981 to 2025.

In the conservative scenario, income per family per season went from S/ 1,725 to S/ 3,757. Seasons with heavy losses fell from 3 in 10 to under 1 in 20. The risk of losing almost everything fell from 6% to 0.4%. The pest risk index fell 32%. Of every 100 families, 93 earn more and the rest stay about the same with less risk. When the local market saturates, coordinating holds the price drop to around 1% instead of 5%. In an El Niño year like 2015, the current potato rotation would have returned 70 to 74% of the possible harvest, while the plan we suggest, with quinoa and tarwi, would have returned 93 to 96%. A plan for a community of 10 families takes about 8 seconds to compute.

What we hope it changes

In the short term, a plan a Colca family can act on this season. Over time, as more families join, Qullqa becomes a living map of Andean farming. With their consent, the admin panel turns anonymised data into risk maps and a “where to go first” view for agricultural technicians, along with seasonal rainfall, frost and El Niño trends. That lets authorities send canals, soil support and technical help toward the families who contributed the data in the first place. We never sell the data.

What we built it with

An installable web app (PWA) in React, a Node.js and Fastify server, and PostgreSQL with PostGIS for the spatial side. The decision engine is written in TypeScript as a pure module with automated tests. It runs on a Microsoft Azure virtual machine. We reach satellite data through NASA Earthdata and Microsoft Planetary Computer, and we designed the interface in Figma.

Where the creativity is

We moved the unit of decision from the farm to the community. That let us borrow from game theory, with a rule that makes cooperation safe to join, and then translate the result into ayni, something these communities already practise, instead of handing out money. We also treat farmers’ phones as field instruments for everything satellites miss at the scale of one plot, and we corrected a known rainfall bias for this specific valley rather than trusting a global product as it comes.

What we thought hard about

Privacy between neighbours came first. What each family cares about stays private, and neighbours only ever see plot borders and the shared plan. We also refused to build a black box, so every recommendation comes with three options, its sources and a confidence level.

Honesty is a design rule for us, not a disclaimer. Qullqa never turns an estimate into a fact, a correlation into a cause, or a simulation into a proven prediction. Every number says where it came from and whether it was measured, estimated, simulated or assumed, and every screen reminds the user that the tool supports the decision and does not replace their experience or an agricultural technician’s.

Then there is who actually uses it. Large type, every icon paired with its word, a phone number and a 4 digit PIN with a recovery code, joining a community by name with no leader and no invite codes, and installation straight from the browser.

What is still missing

Right now we only compute plans for the Colca corridor, and every new valley needs its data processed first. Prices, costs and yields still need calibrating with INIA and local market data. As it stands the model prefers quinoa and tarwi over potato more than is realistic, and it is too hard on cabanita maize. The families in our simulation are invented, the prices are catalogue averages, and for subsistence families part of the income gain is food they no longer have to buy rather than money in hand. Next we want to test with real Colca families, add more valleys, bring in 30 m NDVI from HLS, soil moisture from SMAP and climate scenarios from NEX GDDP CMIP6, add audio in Quechua, and publish on the Play Store.
